title: I Built a $600 Gaming PC That Actually Runs Everything
creator: Drift Tech
description:
$598 in parts, 1080p high settings, 60+ fps in every game I tested. Full parts list below.

Download Ember Legends for free and get the starter pack: https://emberlegends.gg/drift

PARTS
CPU: Ryzen 5 7600 ($179)
Motherboard: B650 ($109)
RAM: 32GB DDR5-6000 ($85)
SSD: 1TB NVMe ($55)
GPU: RX 6700 XT, used ($220)
Case + PSU: reused from my old build

sentences.t: Six hundred dollars.
That's the budget, and the goal is a PC that plays every big game at 1080p, high settings, sixty frames or better.
A few years ago, that would've been a joke.
Today, I think it's actually doable, but only if you're willing to be a little bit sneaky.
So let's go through the parts list, and I'll tell you where I saved and where I absolutely did not.
Starting with the CPU, I went with a Ryzen 5 7600.
It's six cores, twelve threads, and it was on sale for a hundred and seventy-nine dollars.
Could I have gone cheaper with last generation's chips?
Sure, but the AM5 platform means you can drop in a much faster CPU in three or four years without changing the motherboard.
That's the kind of saving that doesn't show up on day one.
Motherboard, a basic B650 board for a hundred and nine dollars.
No fancy lights, no WiFi seven, nothing you don't need.
It's got two M.2 slots and decent power delivery, and that's it.
Memory, thirty-two gigs of DDR5 at six thousand, two sticks, eighty-five dollars.
I know some people will say sixteen is enough, and for a lot of games right now, it is.
But the price difference was twenty bucks, and newer games are getting hungrier every year.
Storage, a one-terabyte NVMe drive for fifty-five dollars.
It's not the fastest drive on the market, but you will genuinely not notice the difference while gaming.
Now, the graphics card, which is where most of the budget goes.
I found a used RX 6700 XT on a local marketplace for two hundred and twenty dollars.
And yes, I know, buying used is scary.
So here's what I do.
Meet in person, ask the seller to run a benchmark in front of you, and look at the fans and the ports for damage.
This one ran a full loop of a stress test at normal temperatures, and the seller even had the original box.
New, that card would be about a hundred dollars more.
For the case, I'm reusing the one from my old build, and the power supply is a six-hundred-fifty-watt gold unit I already had.
If you're buying those new, add about a hundred and twenty dollars, and you're slightly over budget, but not by much.
So the total, for the parts I actually bought, comes to five hundred and ninety-eight dollars.
Two dollars to spare.
I'm going to spend it on a coffee.
The build itself went smoothly, except for the part where I forgot to plug in the CPU power cable and spent ten minutes staring at a black screen.
Classic.
And speaking of games, this video is brought to you by Ember Legends.
Ember Legends is a free-to-play fantasy RPG that you can play on your phone or on PC, and your progress carries over between the two.
The story is that the world's last dragon has been killed, and every kingdom is fighting over what's left of its fire.
You build a team of heroes from over two hundred characters, each with their own abilities, and take them into turn-based battles.
And this is not one of those games where you just mash auto-battle and watch.
The fights are actually tactical, so you have to think about turn order, elemental weaknesses, and which hero is going to soak up the damage.
I've been playing it on the new PC for the last couple of weeks, and it runs at a locked hundred and forty-four frames.
The art style is gorgeous, every hero has this hand-painted look, and the ultimate attacks have big animated cinematics.
My favorite hero right now is a fire mage named Seraphine, who can chain burning damage across the whole enemy team, and when she gets going, it's absolute chaos.
There's also a guild system, so you can team up with friends, take on raid bosses together, and trade gear.
My guild is called Budget Builders, and we are, I'll be honest, mid at best.
But it's fun, and the community is surprisingly friendly.
I've had people in my guild message me at two in the morning asking for team advice, and honestly, I've done the same thing to them.
There's a PvP arena too, if you want to test your team against other players, with seasonal rankings and rewards.
And there's a new event running right now called the Ashfall Festival, which has its own story chapter and an exclusive hero you can unlock just by playing.
The game gets a content update every month, so there's always something new to do.
Last month they added a whole new region, a frozen archipelago with its own heroes, its own boss, and a story that actually made me want to finish it.
And if you're worried about pay-to-win, I've been playing completely free, and my team is holding its own in the arena.
Now, the part you actually care about.
If you download Ember Legends using the link in the description, you'll get a starter pack with fifty thousand gold, ten summon scrolls, and an epic hero of your choice.
That's a really strong head start, because it took me about a week to earn that much on my own account.
Those summon scrolls are the main way you get new heroes, so having ten of them on day one is a big deal.
There's also a daily login reward, so even if you just open the game for a minute, you're building toward something.
On top of that, if you reach level ten in your first seven days, you unlock a bonus legendary summon.
The game is completely free to download, on iOS, Android, and PC.
And the link works like a promo code, so you'll get the rewards automatically, and you don't need to type anything in.
Again, that's the link in the description, or you can scan the QR code on screen right now.
Give it a shot, and if you join, look for the Budget Builders guild, because we need all the help we can get.
Thanks to Ember Legends for supporting the channel.
Okay, benchmarks, the moment of truth.
Cyberpunk at 1080p, high settings, no ray tracing, averaged sixty-eight frames.
Turn on FSR quality mode, and that jumps to about eighty-five.
Fortnite on high, around a hundred and sixty.
Baldur's Gate 3 on ultra, sixty-two in the city, which is the toughest part of that game.
And temperatures stayed under seventy-five degrees on both the CPU and the GPU, even after an hour.
So, did we hit the goal?
Yes, comfortably, in every game I tried.
The one caveat is that this relies on finding a good used graphics card, and that takes a bit of patience.
If you want everything new, budget about seven hundred.
The full parts list is in the description, with the prices I paid.
Let me know what you'd change in the comments, and I'll see you in the next build.
